sources.title: Mark Goresky, Lecture Notes on Sheaves and Perverse Sheaves, version of June 26, 2026
sources.locator: Sections read in the full 168-page PDF (text extracted with MuPDF): 1(d) local systems and locally constant sheaves pp. 5-7; 2.1-2.3 simplicial sheaves and cochain cohomology pp. 10-11; 3.3 quasi-isomorphism invariance pp. 14-15; 7.3-7.4 exact sequences of a pair pp. 21-23; 8.1-8.11 stratifications, Whitney conditions, normal slices and links, the first isotopy lemma, control data and triangulation pp. 24-30; 9.1-9.4 constructible sheaves and the bounded constructible derived category pp. 30-32.

contents.name: 8.1-8.2, pp. 24-25: stratifications, the frontier axiom and Whitney condition B for a pair of strata
8.3-8.4, pp. 25-27: normal slice, link L_Y(y) and the local structure U_y = cone(L_Y) x B^1
8.5, p. 27: first isotopy lemma - a proper stratified submersion is locally trivial
8.7-8.8, pp. 27-28: existence of control data (Thom-Mather) and the isotopy-lemma paradigm
8.10, pp. 28-29: Whitney stratifications of complex algebraic varieties; triangulation smooth on strata with stratum closures as subcomplexes
8.11, p. 29: canonical weak deformation retraction onto a stratum
contents.reason: The retraction and its specialisation properties are consumed by the later six-operations and perverse pairs of this frontier; the cone chart and control data on this page do not require the retraction.

contents.name: 9.1-9.2, p. 30: constructible sheaves, algebraic constructibility and the bounded constructible derived category D_c^b(W)
9.3, p. 30: finite hypercohomology of compact cohomologically constructible complexes
9.4, pp. 31-32: Verdier duality on the constructible derived category
contents.reason: Duality is constructed in the later analytic six-operations pair of this same frontier; this page only needs finite incidence and local cohomology models.

sources.title: John Mather, Notes on Topological Stability (Harvard lecture notes, July 1970; published as Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 49 (2012), 475-506)
sources.locator: Sections 1-2 (Whitney conditions a and b), 5 (Whitney pre-stratifications), 6 (tubular neighbourhoods), 7 (control data), 9 (controlled vector fields) and 10-11 (parameter groups, first and second isotopy lemmas) of the 1970 Harvard notes scan; text layer read with MuPDF and headings cross-checked against the printed section numbers.

contents.name: 1: Condition a and its invariance under diffeomorphism
2: Condition b, the implication (b) => (a) and the dimension drop dim Y < dim X
5: Whitney pre-stratifications and the frontier condition
6: tubular neighbourhoods: existence, uniqueness up to isomorphism, and compatibility with a submersion
7: control data - definition and the existence theorem (Proposition 7.1) with prescribed submanifold constraints
9: controlled vector fields and the existence of fields satisfying prescribed control conditions (Proposition 9.1)
10: local one-parameter groups generated by controlled fields; proper controlled submersions are locally trivial fibrations (Corollaries 10.2-10.4)
11: Thom's first isotopy lemma (Proposition 11.1), second isotopy lemma (Proposition 11.2) and control data over a system (Proposition 11.3)
3-4: blowing up the diagonal and the intrinsic formulation of condition b
contents.reason: The intrinsic fat-square formulation is a proof device for Mather's development; the library proof uses the equivalent sequence formulation in local coordinates.

contents.name: 8: abstract pre-stratified sets and morphisms of pre-stratified sets
contents.reason: Abstract pre-stratified set formalism is not needed for the concrete Euclidean and algebraic statements scaffolded here.

sources.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (v6.10, November 2024)
sources.locator: Chapter 2(l) Noether normalisation theorem 2.45; Chapter 4(i) nonsingularity and regularity; Chapter 5(j),(p) dimension and smooth maps; Chapter 8(a),(b) normal varieties, finiteness of integral closure (Proposition 8.3) and the normalisation of a variety.

contents.name: 2(l): Noether normalisation theorem (2.45), finiteness of a k-algebra over a polynomial subalgebra
4(i): nonsingularity and regularity; regular local rings and smoothness over a perfect field
8(a)-(b): integral closure of a finitely generated domain in a finite field extension is finite (8.3); normalisation of a variety and normal curves are nonsingular
5(j) and 6(p): dimensions of varieties and fibres of morphisms
contents.reason: Dimension theory is already published on the prerequisite dimension and fibre pages of this frontier; this pair consumes it only through the cited published items.

contents.name: 3.H, pp. 327-334: local coefficients via modules over the group ringoid; homology and cohomology with local coefficients
3.H: cellular chains and cochains with local coefficients and their naturality under cellular maps
Chapter 0, pp. 5-8: CW complexes, cell complexes and finite cell structures
contents.reason: CW complexes and their cellular chain complexes are already published on the prerequisite algebraic-topology pages; only the local-coefficient comparison is consumed here.

sources.title: Mark Goresky, Lecture Notes on Sheaves and Perverse Sheaves, version of June 26, 2026
sources.locator: Section 5.4 (Finite type), p. 20 of the 168-page PDF; Section 8.10 (triangulation of Whitney stratified sets), pp. 28-29.

contents.name: 5.4, p. 20: a space has finite type if it is homeomorphic to K - L with K a finite simplicial complex and L a closed subcomplex
8.10, pp. 28-29: Whitney stratified sets admit triangulations smooth on each stratum with closures as subcomplexes
contents.reason: The existence of compatible finite triangulations is proved on the companion A page of this batch; the example only exhibits why a deleted boundary is necessary for such a convention.

sources.title: Allen Hatcher, Algebraic Topology (2002)
sources.locator: Theorem 2B.3 proof (S^n as the one-point compactification of R^n); Section 1.A, compactness of a graph with finitely many vertices and edges; Chapter 0, finite cell complexes.

contents.name: Theorem 2B.3 proof: S^n is viewed as the one-point compactification of R^n
1.A: a graph with finitely many vertices and edges is compact as a continuous image of a compact space; compact subsets meet only finitely many edges
Chapter 0: finite cell complexes and cellular attachments
contents.reason: General CW machinery is not used by this two-step example; the compactness input is the published finite-simplicial-complex property.
